subjects.question: Why would a city need marks on clay?
subjects.summary: Making a city work meant bringing food, materials and labor together. At Uruk, marks on clay helped institutions retain information about goods and their allocation. The selected tablet, dated c. 3100–2900 BCE and only probably from Uruk, makes this work tangible. It is a small administrative object within a much longer urban history, not a founding certificate for writing or civilization.

sections.title: Food and skilled work behind the monuments
sections.text: Southern Mesopotamian communities farmed, fished and used river landscapes long before the selected tablet was made. By around 3200 BCE, Uruk had large mud-brick buildings and elaborate crafts. Building and supplying such places brought producers, makers and administrators into relationships of dependence. Accounts of goods and workers’ rations give one view of that organization. They make the institution’s requirements unusually visible, while a household’s own priorities are harder to recover from these records.

sections.title: A record separates a thing from its amount
sections.text: Look first at the photograph: some marks were cut into the surface, others pressed as round depressions, and lines divide parts of the clay. The catalogue identifies pictographs and numerical impressions. It interprets the tablet as probably concerning grain deliveries and distributions, but warns that missing verbs make a precise reading difficult. The diagram separates categories, quantities and recordkeeping as analytical tasks. It supplies no numerical translation, named recipient or complete itinerary for this particular account.

sections.title: Storage, allocation and power
sections.text: Clay gave an account a durable, movable surface. Recording an obligation or allocation could make it available beyond the moment of exchange and to someone who was not there. Spar links early economic recording with large institutional estates. That is a mechanism connecting administration with food and work, not proof that all grain passed through one central store. Nor does the presence of rations alone tell us whether a particular person was enslaved, employed seasonally or supported as a dependent.

sections.title: The city continued after this tablet
sections.text: The end of the object’s date range is not the end of Uruk. Later city rulers, walls and literary traditions belong to different evidence and dates. Excavators also studied residential quarters, especially from later millennia. Those houses can enrich the city’s long history, but cannot simply be projected backward as the homes of the people represented by this account. Compare Uruk with Dholavira and Liangzhu by asking who coordinated work and what survives of it.

deeperReading.text: An allocation records something an institution chose to count. It does not describe all the effort needed to turn grain into food, care for dependents or maintain a dwelling. Those are questions to investigate through domestic deposits, tools and dated building contexts, rather than answers supplied by the tablet. The DAI account explains why the surviving research picture is uneven: much excavation concentrated on monumental architecture, while the residential quarters it discusses are predominantly later. The absence of a person’s voice in an account should therefore shape the question we ask, not license an invented biography.

Similar-looking recordkeeping needs in distant societies do not prove that one borrowed from another, or that all communities needed the same institutions to organize work.

subjects.question: Why put scenes of work and play beside the dead?
subjects.summary: An elite chapel wall at Saqqara shows offerings, music and a game. Behind such representations lay work: growing and processing food, moving materials, keeping records and sustaining institutions. Settlement archaeology at Giza and a crew’s logbook open different windows onto that organization, at their own places and dates.

sections.title: Providing for the dead
sections.text: Nikauhor and Sekhemhathor’s wall belongs to a funerary chapel, not an occupied household. Its false doors marked places for offerings and prayers. Images of offerings were intended to provide for the dead. The museum interprets the pictured senet game as a possible afterlife journey. It also identifies displaced and erased elements: this particular wall changed before reaching its present arrangement.

sections.title: A building project needed a town
sections.text: At Giza, AERA’s excavations investigate a Fourth Dynasty settlement supporting royal construction. Workshops, kitchens, storage areas and administrators’ houses made different tasks depend on one another. Tools needed making and repair; people needed shelter and meals. Materials arrived by waterways during inundation and by other transport at different times. These remains concern Giza, not the selected Saqqara chapel.

sections.title: Grain was only a beginning
sections.text: Stored grain still had to become food. Excavated bread molds, floor-set vats, hearths and ash help AERA investigate mixing and baking. The project interprets large production as repeated small bakery units within a royal institution. Preparing meals therefore required equipment, fuel and continuing labor, alongside agricultural production. A silo alone could not feed a workforce.

One entry also records a boat sent to obtain food from Heliopolis. Such administrative writing joins movement to provisioning rather than simply celebrating a finished monument. The surviving record does not explain how every block was raised or establish every crew member’s freedom.

sections.title: Work continued after construction
sections.text: Institutions changed as projects ended. AERA interprets settlement near Menkaure’s temple and Khentkawes’ monument as a shift toward maintaining deceased rulers’ cults. Rebuilding, abandonment and reoccupation complicate a single ending story. Ritual service still required buildings, people and supplies. This proposed local sequence is neither the history of every Egyptian settlement nor a precise timetable for every resident.

Seasonal water had to be captured and stored; stone-built remains let us investigate how this work fitted into the city. sections.title: A city needs water between rains
sections.text: Khadir’s seasonal streams supplied an urban settlement in a dry setting. Reservoirs to the east and south of the citadel, together with drains, made water management part of the built city. Capture and storage address different problems: water must first reach a place where it can be held, and the store must remain usable. The remains establish investment in those tasks; they do not preserve a complete operating manual or tell us how much each household received.

sections.title: Makers and residents used the city too
sections.text: Bead workshops and objects of shell, stone, copper and other materials bring skilled production into the account. Housing varied in size and quality, and distinct fortified sectors structured movement and access. Such differences support questions about inequality. They do not give us a census of occupations, a named ruler or proof that every person within one sector had the same social position.

subjects.question: How can waterworks and burials tell different parts of a story?
subjects.summary: Liangzhu’s rice-growing communities changed a wet landscape with dams, channels and earthen construction. Water control supported production and movement, while elaborate burials and jade reveal unequal status. These are related ways into the city’s history, with different kinds of evidence behind each. Neither a dam nor the selected cong gives a direct account of the decisions, household labor or beliefs of every resident.

sections.title: The city belonged to a wider landscape
sections.text: The archaeological property includes high dams near valley mouths, low dams on the plain, the city and Yaoshan. Rice cultivation supported this regional society. The city’s earthen monuments and differentiated cemeteries put authority and belief into the landscape alongside farming. Looking beyond the urban centre matters: a large built place depended on work and resources beyond its monumental core. The UNESCO frame of c. 3300–2300 BCE describes a site sequence, rather than the life of one unchanging government.

sections.title: Engineering involved materials and repeated work

Channels and controlled access points also helped move people and materials. The conceptual diagram identifies storage, channels and productive activity without supplying a traced ancient canal route. Building and maintaining a system would have had to coexist with agricultural work; the paper’s proposed labor totals are estimates based on assumptions, not surviving attendance lists.

Nor does a water-control system alone prove one universal form of coercive government. A next investigation should test how benefits, burdens and access varied, rather than treating the finished dam as an explanation of its own labor arrangements. Household and gender histories need more direct evidence than this bounded set currently supplies.

People constructed and altered these places over centuries. UNESCO’s approximate 3000–1800 BCE development range describes a sequence, rather than one founding date or a date for every wall. Built gathering places help us ask how people assembled and organized work; their scale alone does not identify the person directing each task.

subjects.question: What survives when a household was built in stone?
subjects.summary: Stone furnishings make household tasks visible at Skara Brae. A home needed heat, storage, food and continuing maintenance, while its links with neighboring houses changed. The surviving interiors bring together several ancient phases and modern repair; they are not a single untouched moment.

sections.title: A home needed places for different tasks
sections.text: Skara Brae brings household space into view through stone. A central hearth, slab-built enclosures and a shelved structure conventionally called a dresser organize the surviving interiors. These features invite practical questions: where could heat be supplied, belongings kept and people accommodated? The names help us begin, while their particular uses need interpretation. A stone frame survives differently from the bedding, fuel, food and other materials that people brought into a home.

sections.title: Building made a settlement, not just separate rooms
sections.text: The houses used flat slabs and stood within accumulated midden material. Their occupants worked within a built environment that changed through occupation. Moving between houses also required passages and entrances. These connections were not simply one complete plan laid down at the beginning: gaps developed into passages, and roofing was added during occupation. Maintaining a home therefore involved relationships with adjacent buildings as well as work inside its walls.

HES also describes farming, hunting and fishing within village life. Reading these different records together connects domestic space with work in the surrounding landscape, without pretending that one sample supplies a complete menu.

The coast changed too. The present shore should orient a visitor today, rather than serve as an exact drawing of the environment experienced during village occupation.

subjects.question: Can a pot identify the person buried beside it?
subjects.summary: A carefully finished beaker opens a wider inquiry into Nubian production, households and institutions. At Kerma, excavated craft installations and residential spaces place skilled work beside government and worship. This particular vessel was found at Abydos in Egypt; its documented context and the proposed identity of its owner remain different questions.

sections.title: Skilled hands controlled contrasting surfaces
sections.text: The beaker’s dark upper surface and red body began with choices about clay, finishing and fire. The Met describes hand-forming, red ocher and polishing before firing. Inverting vessels in combustible material helped create reducing conditions for the black top and interior. These were connected operations that makers had to manage. The irregular boundary is visible in the photograph; the proposed coating and firing explanation come from the catalogue, rather than being established by color alone.

sections.title: A capital organized different kinds of work
sections.text: Kerma was an independent Nubian capital with institutions beyond pottery production. Excavators identified residential quarters, royal buildings, administrative spaces, a circular audience hall and chapels around the principal temple. Craft installations occurred in several areas, especially near places of worship. Metalworking, faience and ceramics belonged to this setting. Placing those activities together shows how making, meeting and religious practice occupied an organized city; it does not establish that a king personally directed every workshop or that every worker had the same status.

sections.title: Provisioning linked homes with the surrounding land
sections.text: The project’s residential account describes buildings arranged around courtyards, with kitchens, silos and other domestic annexes. Storing supplies and preparing meals gave household work a place in the city’s fabric. The broader livelihood account includes herding, plant resources, hunting and fishing. This setting helps explain why a finished vessel belongs in a history of production and provision, alongside the monumental buildings. It does not tell us the contents of this particular beaker, the share of each food in a diet or who performed each household task.

sections.title: An Egyptian findspot opens a further question
sections.text: The selected vessel has its own history: the museum dates it around 1802–1640 BCE and records its discovery in Abydos tomb 525. Kerma ceramics and Egyptian goods occur together in comparable graves. The museum proposes that some owners might have been traders from Kerma living in Egypt. That possibility makes an interesting research question, but the ceramic tradition does not identify an individual’s birthplace, language or occupation. The documented grave is firmer evidence than the proposed biography.

sections.title: Exchange and political relationships changed
sections.text: The Met’s regional chronology describes both trade and conflict between Kerma and Egypt. Imported objects entered elite tombs beside locally made equipment, while rulers negotiated alliances and contested control farther north. Later Egyptian campaigns changed the political setting. Keeping this sequence visible gives objects a changing institutional context instead of treating Nubia as a timeless source of distinctive pottery. Neither a traveled vessel nor a later Kushite royal name proves that the same government continued unchanged from Kerma to Taharqo’s much later reign.

packs.title: Communities, cities and the evidence of work
packs.question: How do we know about early communities, work, exchange and political organization?
packs.orientation: Begin with things people made and places they built. A grain account, a tomb wall, a reservoir, a carved jade and a stone household preserve different kinds of human activity. Some societies built large cities; others organized life differently. Their histories are contemporary without forming a single ladder toward civilization.
packs.geography: Move among southern Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley, Gujarat, the lower Yangtze, coastal Peru and Orkney. River systems, arid landscapes and island settings invite different questions. The selected object’s place attribution is kept separate from the location of a wider society.
packs.limits: This is a selective investigation of archaeological and institutional evidence. Many communities beyond these places are absent. Large monuments and durable materials survive unevenly; they cannot stand for all early human life.

Americas.reason: Caral now has settlement, food-evidence and construction-renewal explanation with phased context. One Supe study and selected project pages do not complete wider American or household histories.

Africa.reason: The selected Saqqara wall now connects to a bounded source-based account of provisioning, Giza institutions and changing cult service. Wider Nile farming, households, gender and provincial histories remain selective.

Europe.reason: Skara Brae now has household/landscape interpretation, source-qualified phases and an original feature guide. Wider Neolithic Europe, measured plans and independent archaeological review remain open.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Uruk account with distinct urban chronology, accounting diagram and source interpretation. Later residential evidence is not backdated; wider Mesopotamian and household histories remain open.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Dholavira water/work inquiry separates excavated components from proposed radar features. The regional seal has no asserted Dholavira findspot. Wider Indus reference history remains open.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Liangzhu account joins rice, waterworks and jade while preserving separate dates and corrected capacity estimates. Household relations and wider East Asian histories remain open.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: A sourced Kuk reference supplies a highland New Guinea agricultural setting from about 2400 BCE. Earlier C1 dates and mainland Southeast Asian settings still need research. The later Lapita dossier is a comparison, not contemporary C1 settlement evidence.

comparisons.question: How do accounts and waterworks make different kinds of urban work visible?
Whose work becomes visible in a record or an image?
How did communities organize work around water?
What can built spaces tell us about gathering and household work?
How did food production and building renewal require continuing work, and which records make it visible?
How can we distinguish commemoration, occupied space and later rebuilding when investigating daily work?

orientations.title: Supe Valley: public buildings and the work of feeding people
orientations.question: How can buildings and food traces tell different parts of a community’s history?

summary.title: Coast and valley
summary.text: Caral’s platforms and circular courts place collective building beside a less visible history of food production. Coastal Áspero offers a second setting in the Supe Valley. Comparing them connects monumental spaces with the plants people used, without assuming that every household had the same diet or role.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: platforms and recessed circular courts

sections.title: Provisioning leaves several kinds of evidence
sections.text: The dental-calculus study recovered plant starches from nine people at Áspero and one at Caral. These traces bring food use into an account otherwise dominated by large buildings. The authors consider exchange as one possible explanation for access to some plants. Starch presence is not a measure of the calories supplied by a crop.

citations.locator: Abstract; Discussion: exchange and limits of starch ubiquity

sections.title: Buildings accumulated over time
sections.text: Caral’s urban plan and ceremonial architecture developed over centuries within the broad 3000–1800 BCE frame. A visitor’s view gathers different building episodes. The arrangement supports questions about organized work, but cannot by itself tell us who assigned tasks, whether people volunteered, or how work varied between households.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis, criterion (ii), Integrity and Authenticity

orientations.perspectives: Builders and food producers left material traces, not a complete set of personal accounts. A small sample of human remains cannot speak for all valley residents.
orientations.scope: A coastal–inland comparison within the Supe Valley, not an account of every American community. Burial samples and building phases have their own dates within the wider site frame.

activity.prompt: Use the account above to choose evidence for two questions: what plants some people consumed, and how public gathering spaces were arranged. What could neither source tell you?
activity.response: Starches address plant use; platforms and courts address spatial arrangement. Neither supplies every household’s diet or a named worker’s explanation of their obligations. Explain the mismatch rather than treating the two sources as interchangeable.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE lies within Caral’s broadly dated development. Platforms and circular gathering spaces orient us to the Supe Valley’s built landscape. They do not establish the same layout or activity in every year; the linked coastal food study has separately dated burial contexts.

orientations.title: Nile communities: building, supply and different centres of power
orientations.question: What had to happen around a monument to keep people working?

summary.title: Giza, Saqqara and Kerma
summary.text: Royal monuments depended on food, tools, storage and skilled labor. Giza’s excavated settlement exposes some of that supporting work; Saqqara’s chapel wall presents elite commemoration. Farther south, Kerma developed as a distinct Nubian centre. These places belong to connected Nile histories, not one undifferentiated Egyptian society.

citations.locator: Fourth Dynasty settlement and support staff

sections.title: Supply was part of construction
sections.text: AERA identifies bakeries, kitchens, workshops and storage at Giza. Grain held in royal silos could be distributed for bread and beer; raw materials also arrived for tools and furnishings. This explains a chain of provisioning behind construction. It does not identify every worker’s legal status or make one crew representative of all labor in Egypt.

citations.locator: Settlement account: support staff, materials and grain silos

sections.title: Changing places, separate dates
sections.text: The selected Saqqara wall dates to about 2465–2389 BCE, later than much Fourth Dynasty pyramid building. Kerma’s project dates its city’s foundation around 2500 BCE, while warning that continuity from the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement is unproved. Neither the wall nor a later Kerma beaker dates the beginning of an entire society.

citations.locator: City of Kerma: foundation and uncertain continuity

orientations.perspectives: Excavated work spaces and an elite tomb image answer different questions. The surviving records do not give equal access to administrators, cooks, craftspeople and their families.
orientations.scope: Selected Egyptian and Nubian settings in the later third millennium BCE. Kerma’s later urban layout and the beaker’s second-millennium date are not projected back to 2400 BCE.

activity.prompt: Explain one link between grain storage and monument building. Then name a question about the workers that a grain silo cannot settle.
activity.response: Storage could support regular food preparation for a workforce. That material connection does not reveal a particular worker’s motives, freedom, household circumstances or membership in a named crew.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE falls within the selected Saqqara wall’s museum date range and after Kerma’s approximate foundation. The chapel is evidence of elite funerary representation; Kerma offers a distinct Nubian urban history. The later beaker is a next reading, not an object from this same moment.

citations.locator: City of Kerma: c2500 BCE foundation

orientations.title: Orkney: homes, gathering places and a landscape beyond one village
orientations.question: Why does the end of a settlement not end the history of its landscape?

summary.title: More than the standing houses
summary.text: Skara Brae’s stone rooms and connected passages reveal domestic arrangements. Maeshowe, the Stones of Stenness and the Ring of Brodgar provide different kinds of built spaces in Orkney. Reading homes alongside burial and ceremonial monuments expands the inquiry beyond one village, while keeping each site’s chronology separate.

sections.title: Construction connects household and communal work
sections.text: The village’s fitted stone furnishings organize cooking, storage and sleeping within compact rooms. Larger tombs and stone circles required different construction tasks. Comparing these remains helps us distinguish domestic from communal settings; the surviving stones do not recover every ceremony or the identity of those who directed the work.

sections.title: A later landscape is not a longer village occupation
sections.text: UNESCO describes an Orkney cultural-landscape tradition around 3000–2000 BCE. That broader range continues after the selected Skara Brae occupation. Some standing stones were re-erected in modern times. Today’s view therefore combines prehistoric construction, losses and conservation rather than presenting one unchanged Neolithic moment.

orientations.perspectives: Architecture reveals possible activities more readily than people’s names or beliefs. A ceremonial interpretation is not a recovered script for the event.
orientations.scope: Orkney is a justified local focus: unusually varied surviving domestic and monumental evidence makes comparison possible. It does not represent every European farming community.

activity.prompt: Separate three statements: a stone bed survives; people probably slept there; we know who slept there. Which is observation, which is interpretation, and which needs evidence not supplied?
activity.response: The bed’s form is material evidence; sleeping is a functional interpretation. A named occupant needs further evidence. Apply the same distinction when interpreting a stone circle.

snapshots.text: The 2400 BCE view uses Orkney’s broader 3000–2000 BCE monumental-landscape frame. It does not extend Skara Brae’s village occupation to this date. Read the earlier houses alongside burial and ceremonial monuments, whose individual construction histories remain separate.

citations.locator: Printed p17: modeled village ending 2545–2440 cal BCE

orientations.title: Southern Mesopotamia: institutions, work and durable accounts
orientations.question: How did counting goods become part of organizing a city?

summary.title: Uruk and its surrounding settlements
summary.text: Uruk grew within a landscape of rivers, farming and neighboring settlements. Large institutions handled goods and workers’ rations. Recording quantities on clay made some transactions durable, leaving an unusually visible administrative history alongside buildings and crafted objects.

sections.title: An account serves a practical task
sections.text: The museum’s writing essay connects early tablets with the recording and distribution of resources. Grain, fish and animals could be counted with signs, while names and actions were harder to interpret. This supports an explanation of record keeping as institutional work; it does not make every tablet a complete narrative of a transaction.

citations.locator: Accounting; signs for rations and interpretive limits

sections.title: Political forms changed while cities continued
sections.text: The Uruk account distinguishes late-fourth-millennium growth from the later Early Dynastic city-states, conventionally about 2900–2350 BCE. It describes rulers seeking imported luxury goods through trade or conquest. A tablet dated about 3100–2900 BCE therefore cannot name the rulers or record all political relations of the 2400 BCE world.

orientations.perspectives: Administrative records privilege what institutions counted. They are thinner evidence for unrecorded household labor and for people’s own explanations of their lives.
orientations.scope: A local urban–hinterland focus explains accounting through related settlement and institutional evidence. It is not a claim that writing arose once, or that all West and Central Asia followed Uruk’s sequence.

activity.prompt: A tablet counts grain but gives no clear action word. Give one defensible conclusion and one conclusion that would need more evidence.
activity.response: It records a quantity associated with grain. Whether that quantity was received, owed or issued may remain uncertain; a particular worker’s biography is still farther beyond the account.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE sits within the museum’s Early Dynastic city-state frame. Uruk continued after the earlier spread of its material culture. The selected grain tablet is older: use it to investigate accounting practices, not as a direct record of this selected year.

orientations.title: Indus settlements: managing water in different places
orientations.question: How did water problems shape the work of building a city?

summary.title: Dholavira and Mohenjo-daro
summary.text: Dholavira stood on arid Khadir Island, where seasonal streams and storage mattered. Mohenjo-daro developed beside the Indus, with brick streets, wells and drainage. Their surviving structures let us compare ways of organizing water and inhabited space without assuming identical environments or government.

citations.locator: Description: seasonal streams and water management
Brief synthesis: location, wells and drainage

sections.title: Storage and drainage answer different needs
sections.text: At Dholavira, capturing scarce seasonal water was part of the city’s infrastructure. At Mohenjo-daro, wells and drains formed part of its built layout. Keeping water available and moving unwanted water away are distinct practical tasks. Their remains invite questions about construction and maintenance, but do not identify one ruler who controlled every system.

sections.title: A plan gathers several histories
sections.text: Dholavira’s long occupation and the selected seal’s narrower date range should not be merged. Nor does the regional seal’s collection attribution make it a Dholavira excavation find. Mohenjo-daro’s later Buddhist stupa is a separate addition to the ancient city landscape; it belongs to a different period from the third-millennium urban remains.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: second-century CE Buddhist stupa

orientations.perspectives: Buildings and workshop remains expose practical activities. Without a fully deciphered script, they do not supply every resident’s account of authority, rights or maintenance duties.
orientations.scope: Two named settlements in different parts of the Indus world. Modern composite plans are not photographs of one simultaneous city layout, and regional object dates are not local construction dates.

activity.prompt: Explain why a reservoir and a drain might both belong in a city. What extra evidence would you need to name the people responsible for maintaining them?
activity.response: Storage retains water for use; drainage carries water away. Their presence supports different infrastructure needs. Administrative records or securely contextualized evidence of labor would be needed to identify particular maintenance arrangements.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE falls within the broad third-millennium Indus urban setting. Compare water management at Dholavira with wells and drainage at Mohenjo-daro. The view marks a regional comparison, not a claim that every visible structure at either site was operating in that exact year.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: third-millennium settlement and urban systems

orientations.title: Lower Yangtze: cultivated land, waterworks and unequal burials
orientations.question: How do landscapes and objects reveal different kinds of organization?

summary.title: Liangzhu and its surrounding landscape
summary.text: Liangzhu’s city, peripheral waterworks and cemeteries belong to a lower-Yangtze landscape supported by rice cultivation. The city site and Yaoshan burial area offer different evidence: built spaces show organized investment, while differences between graves support interpretations of social distinction.

citations.locator: Description; Brief synthesis: four component areas

sections.title: Infrastructure and social interpretation
sections.text: Water-control works connect cultivated land with the settlement’s surroundings. UNESCO interprets the city layout and differentiated burials as evidence of a regional state. That is an archaeological interpretation of surviving patterns, not a contemporary constitution or a recovered list of everyone’s duties.

sections.title: A jade has its own chronology and limits
sections.text: The selected cong is dated around 2400 BCE. Its wider museum culture label extends beyond the city’s approximately 3300–2300 BCE frame. The catalogue treats the object’s exact function and meaning as uncertain; wealth and status are proposed associations. It cannot identify every belief or the experiences of people outside richly furnished graves.

orientations.perspectives: Elaborate objects and differentiated graves make some social distinctions visible. They do not provide equal testimony from farmers, waterworks laborers and those buried with fewer goods.
orientations.scope: A justified local focus compares city, waterworks and burial evidence within one documented landscape. Other East Asian settings require their own histories; this is not a universal sequence from farming to statehood.

activity.prompt: Which question is better answered by a dam system, and which by a burial object: how water was managed, or how objects marked distinctions among the dead? Name a limit of each.
activity.response: Dams address water management but do not name every laborer. Burial objects address funerary distinctions but do not reconstruct every living person’s beliefs. Neither alone is a complete social history.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE lies within Liangzhu’s city-site frame and matches the approximate date assigned to the selected jade. Those overlapping dates make comparison possible; they do not establish that this museum object came from the city excavation or that every waterwork was built at this moment.

orientations.title: Kuk and An Sơn: reading work in buried landscapes
orientations.question: How can ditches, floors and dated deposits reveal different settlement histories?

summary.title: Kuk in the upper Wahgi Valley
summary.text: At Kuk, connected ditches and larger channels redirected water at a wetland margin. Archaeologists interpret this as deliberate preparation for cultivation. This highland setting offers a food-production history whose evidence is different from a city plan, a written account or the later Lapita pottery of island settlements.

citations.locator: Summary of palaeochannels and ditch articulation; drainage for cultivation

sections.title: A mainland comparison with its own sequence
sections.text: At An Sơn in southern Vietnam, the excavators estimate initial occupation around 2500–2200 calibrated BCE. Much of the excavated occupation is later, and the burials later still. Alternating floors and occupation layers suggest houses at ground level, but precise house plans could not be reconstructed. These remains offer a mainland comparison with Kuk; they do not establish migration between the two places.

citations.locator: Introduction: 1997 floors and house interpretation; Chronology: initial and later occupation

sections.title: A network is more than a single cut
sections.text: The investigators describe larger channels receiving water from smaller ditches. Some networks contain right-angled junctions and divisions; others branch differently. Connected cuts make planned drainage a stronger interpretation than an isolated depression would. Shallow cultivation features survive less clearly, so the network does not identify every crop or plot boundary.

citations.locator: Earliest ditch networks; Summary; early network 353

sections.title: Dating a sequence does not fill every year
sections.text: The introduction’s table gives the early Phase 3 range as 4350–3980 calibrated years before 1950, approximately 2400–2030 BCE. Other ditch episodes belong later. The authors lack the precision to date every use of each location. A gap in the dated record cannot simply be filled with an invented uninterrupted sequence.

citations.locator: Subphases: spatial variation and insufficient archaeological precision

orientations.perspectives: Earthworks preserve traces of planning and repeated work. They do not name the cultivators or establish their land rights. Modern communities are not represented by archaeological interpretation alone.
orientations.scope: Two separate settings: the New Guinea highlands and a southern Vietnamese mound. Their overlapping broad dates are not a route or shared political history. Lapita is a later reading destination, not evidence of a 2400 BCE island migration.

activity.prompt: Explain why linked channels support a drainage interpretation. Then distinguish the approximate date range from a claim that every plot was cultivated every year.
activity.response: Smaller ditches joining larger channels provide a route for water to leave the margin. Dated fills and stratigraphy place episodes in broad ranges; they do not establish continuous annual use of every field.

snapshots.text: Around 2400 BCE is near Kuk’s rounded early Phase 3 boundary and within An Sơn’s estimated initial-occupation range. These are independent archaeological chronologies, not exact events in the selected year. An Sơn’s later houses and burials cannot all be assigned to its beginning. Lapita remains a later comparison.
